newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-NIEKRO, LASORDA, FOX, WELLS ENTER HALL OF FAME.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-NIEKRO, LASORDA, FOX, WELLS ENTER HALL OF FAME.

text.p: Phil Niekro, who used his trademark fluttering knuckleball to compile 318 victories over a 24-year career, became the newest member of baseball's Hall of Fame at induction ceremonies Sunday.
Also inducted in the class of 1997 were former Dodgers manager Tommy Lasorda, the late Chicago White Sox second baseman Nellie Fox and former Negro League shortstop Willie Wells.
Niekro was the only choice for enshrinment in regular annual balloting by the baseball writers. The other three inductees were elected by the Veterans Committee.
"I thank my father who taught me how to throw the knuckleball," said Niekro, who spent most of his career with the Braves. "I couldn't break a pane of glass but I won 318 games."
Niekro, who said he waited a long time for the honour, became the 18th 300-game winner in the Hall.

"I think I should have been here sooner, but I'm just glad to finally make it. Like the Braves, if you keep on trying it finally happens," he said of his long-struggling former club, which finally won the World Series in 1995 and is now of of the game's elite teams.
Niekro also credited his sister for helping him to develop his bread and butter pitch.

"My original coaches in the minors helped, but the biggest help was my sister who was the catcher in my backyard," added Niekro, who holds the National League record for putouts by a pitcher (340) and shares the major-league mark for most years with 200 or more innings (19) with the legendary Cy Young.
The 70-year-old Lasorda earned baseball's ultimate honour after managing the Dodgers for 20 years.
"I still bleed Dodger blue, that's for sure," he said.
Lasorda compiled a 1599-1439 record and led Los Angeles to four National League pennants and two World Series titles.
"I still believe God is a Dodger fan," added Lasorda, who paid tribute to the fans Sunday.

"This game does not belong to the owners, it does not belong to the players," he said. "You can have the greatest stadiums in the world and the best baseball team, but if nobody goes through those turnstiles we've got nothing."

Fox was named to 12 All-Star teams and totalled 2,663 hits and a .288 batting average in his 19-year career, which ended in 1965. He was the American League Most Valuable Player in 1959 and won three Gold Gloves. He died in 1975.
Fox's wife, JoAnne, accepted the honour.
"I passionately believe Nellie deserved baseball's highest honour," said his widow. "The support of loyal fans finally got him here."
Wells played for nine Negro League teams from 1924 to 1949 and had a career .331 batting average.
A slick-fielding shortstop nicknamed "The Devil", Wells hit a league-best .403 in 1930 for the St. Louis Stars. A year earlier, Wells led the Negro Leagues with 27 homers.
Wells's daughter, Stella Wells, accepted the honour for her father, who died in 1989.
"My father is the 14th Negro Leagues Player inducted and hopefully there will be many, many more," she said.
